newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks jump as new finmin named.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks jump as new finmin named.

text.p: Thai stocks rallied on Friday as low-profile banker Thanong Bidaya was named the country's new finance minister, but brokers and analysts said the rise was likely to be short-lived.
There was also cautious dealing in the money market as the baht remained soft in the domestic market and slightly firmer in the offshore market, dealers said.
The battered bourse -- which closed at a new 98-month low on Thursday -- ended the day up 3.33 percent after eight consecutive sessions of heavy losses.

Buying was partly fuelled by news that Thanong, chief executive of Thai Military Bank Plc, would fill the finance portfolio left vacant by Amnuay Viravan, who resigned on Thursday over differences with political rivals.
Technical factors were cited as another reason for what was only the bourse's second advance this month, brokers said.

"Investors, including foreigners, bought on expectations that Thanong could run the ministry although he is less popular than his predecessor Amnuay Viravan," said Payuha Boonsiri of Nithipat Capital.
The composite SET index ended 15.48 points up at 480.25 after losing 101.62 points this month alone.
The baht was quoted in the local market at 26.000/26.100 compared with 25.900/26.000 in the morning.
Analysts voiced expectations that the rally would be brief given the long list of economic and political hurdles faced by the country.

"We don't see real buying signals from our local and foreign investors. The gains look suspiciously like a smokescreen that can easily evaporate. We advised our clients to stay on the sidelines," said the marketing head of a major Thai brokerage firm who declined to be named.
Amnuay held the post for less than seven months and was the fifth Thai finance minister to resign in three administrations since 1995.
A broker at Dhana Siam Finance and Securities Plc described the rally as a technical rebound from sharp declines this week aggravated by Amnuay's departure.
"Thanong still needs to take time to assert himself as a finance minister," said Donaldson Hartman, from Salomon Brothers Inc.
Analysts said that on top of deepening property and finance sector problems, Amnuay's resignation renewed speculation that Thailand would eventually be forced to devalue its currency, the baht.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh pledged on Thursday he would retain policies adopted by Amnuay, and the Bank of Thailand would continue its determined defence of the baht.
But analysts said Thanong's appointment on Friday and Chavalit's growing political reliance on his main coalition partner, the Chart Pattana Party, could prompt him to soften the baht policy.
Chart Pattana, led by former premier Chatichai Choonhavan, is known for its past liberal and expansionary policies.
Another broker at Poonpipat Finance and Securities Plc said the new finance minister would have virtually no time to prepare for the first parliamentary debate on the government budget next week.
"Thanong is acceptable although his qualifications do not stand out. He is a second or third-tier choice on the list of prospective candidates that Chavalit has," he said.
